comparison: The notifications plan's F1 (storage, the writer and the scan) against the baseline F0 recorded; inbox-refresh against its S3 form, recorded at F1. Used once: just perf --budgets (tools/perf_check.py, tools/perf-compare.py). Changes are fractions of the baseline's count. Restated where the plan's guess didn't fit its own design, as measured (docs/NOTIFICATIONS_FIX_PLAN.md, F0's budgets).

scan-walk.first.why: the pairing reads the fresh rows once per tier, each batch in its own transaction, so a decision sees the rows as they are (one read of them all before); files_fresh is kept on every new row; the lease and the value guard

import-flush.why: the import ledger's triggers: in the SQLite bundled (3.54), each firing costs a frame of 10-25k instructions even when its WHEN is false, and the import writes a row per statement; two fire per analysis (analysis_import, files_failures_hidden)

pending-import.why: one probe; the larger schema's fixed cost around it (about 1,300 instructions)

inbox-refresh.closed.why: must fall by 90% or more: the ledger's cheap state on the partial index instead of the counts

inbox-refresh.open.why: the counts read while the inbox is shown are linear in the live rows (a count is a scan of the partial index; the bench's ledgers are all new, so both the total and the new are full ranges): only the closed refresh is the cheap state

pending-thumbs.why: the pass's ATTACH parses the catalog's schema, which versions 8 and 9 grew by their tables, indexes and triggers: a fixed cost per pass, not per file
